title: Lab: put numbers into the iron law
summary: Compute the three iron-law terms for one workload, find the dominant one and predict what an upgrade buys.

blocks.md:
The previous lesson gave the iron law in words. Here you use it the way an engineer does: plug in a workload, see which term is largest, and predict what a faster part would actually buy you.

The workload for the whole lab: one accelerator step that **moves 8 GB** of weights and activations over a **2,000 GB/s** memory bus, performs **$10^{11}$ FLOPs** at an effective **100 TFLOP/s** (peak 250 TFLOP/s at 40% utilisation), and pays **0.5 ms** of fixed overhead.

steps.why: The iron law with the three costs paid one after the other.
Bytes divided by bytes per second leaves seconds.
The effective rate already includes utilisation; do not multiply by it twice.
Movement is the largest term, so this step is memory-bound.

blocks.md: Doubling peak compute would shrink only the 1 ms term. Doubling bandwidth shrinks the 4 ms term. The iron law tells you which upgrade to buy **before** you buy it.

blocks.title: Try it: the same workload in the calculator
blocks.md: The calculator starts at the workload above, with the stages run one after the other. Move the bandwidth slider and watch which term leads.

challenge.md: Set bandwidth to **4,000 GB/s** (twice as fast). What is the new total time, in milliseconds?
challenge.hint: Only the movement term changes: 8 GB at 4,000 GB/s.
challenge.explanation: Movement drops from 4 ms to 2 ms; compute (1 ms) and overhead (0.5 ms) stay. 2 + 1 + 0.5 = 3.5 ms. Twice the bandwidth gave 1.57x, not 2x.

blocks.prompt: If movement and compute overlap perfectly (the pipelined bound), what is the best possible time before and after the bandwidth upgrade?
blocks.md: Before: max(4, 1) + 0.5 = **4.5 ms**. After: max(2, 1) + 0.5 = **2.5 ms**. After the upgrade movement is still the slower stage; once it falls below 1 ms, more bandwidth stops helping and compute becomes the wall.

blocks.title: Write the iron law as a function
blocks.md: Complete `iron_law`. With `overlap=False` it returns the sum of the three terms; with `overlap=True` it returns the pipelined bound `max(movement, compute) + overhead`. Units: bytes, bytes/s, FLOPs, FLOP/s, seconds. **Run and check** tests it on the lab's workload.
blocks.code:

t = iron_law(8e9, 2e12, 1e11, 250e12, 0.4, 0.5e-3)
print("sequential:", t)
blocks.check:
assert abs(iron_law(8e9, 2e12, 1e11, 250e12, 0.4, 0.5e-3) - 5.5e-3) < 1e-9, 'sequential time should be 5.5 ms'
assert abs(iron_law(8e9, 2e12, 1e11, 250e12, 0.4, 0.5e-3, overlap=True) - 4.5e-3) < 1e-9, 'pipelined bound should be 4.5 ms'
assert abs(iron_law(8e9, 4e12, 1e11, 250e12, 0.4, 0.5e-3) - 3.5e-3) < 1e-9, 'with 4 TB/s the sum is 3.5 ms'
blocks.hint: `compute = ops / (peak * eta)`; then `return (max(movement, compute) if overlap else movement + compute) + lat`.
blocks.solution:
def iron_law(d_vol, bw, ops, peak, eta, lat, overlap=False):
    movement = d_vol / bw
    compute = ops / (peak * eta)
    core = max(movement, compute) if overlap else movement + compute
    return core + lat


print("sequential:", iron_law(8e9, 2e12, 1e11, 250e12, 0.4, 0.5e-3))
print("pipelined: ", iron_law(8e9, 2e12, 1e11, 250e12, 0.4, 0.5e-3, overlap=True))

questions.q: A dense language model with $N = 10^9$ parameters trains on $D = 2\times10^{10}$ tokens. Using $O \approx 6ND$, how many FLOPs is that, in units of $10^{20}$?
Generating one token with a 7-billion-parameter model costs about $2N$ FLOPs. How many GFLOPs per token?
questions.explanation: 2N = 1.4 × 10¹⁰ FLOP = 14 GFLOP per token, forward pass only.

questions.q: In the lab's workload, which change shortens the sequential time the most?
options: All three save the same time
questions.hint: Compare how many milliseconds each change removes.
questions.explanation: Doubling bandwidth removes 2 ms, doubling compute removes 0.5 ms, halving overhead removes 0.25 ms. Fix the largest term first.

points: The iron law adds movement, compute and overhead; the largest term sets the pace.
An upgrade only helps through the term it shrinks, so it never speeds up the whole by its own factor.
With perfect overlap the bound is max(movement, compute) + overhead.

terms.def: max(movement time, compute time) + overhead: the best case when data movement and computation overlap perfectly
